passages.text: Cubism Art Movement – Overview, Definition, History and Evolution Cubism was an early-20th-century art movement developed in Paris by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, then extended by artists including Juan Gris, Fernand Léger, Jean Metzinger, Albert Gleizes, and Sonia and Robert Delaunay. Rather than copying appearances from one fixed viewpoint, Cubist artists compressed space, fractured forms, and tested how signs and everyday materials could represent objects. This article defines Cubism, traces its main phases and public networks, explains how to recognize its visual logic, and distinguishes core Cubists from precursors and later artists influenced by the movement. What Is Cubism? Cubism is a modern art movement that emerged from the close collaboration between Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in Paris from 1907 onward. They rejected the idea that a painting should behave like a window onto a continuous, three-dimensional world. Instead, they emphasized the flat surface by breaking figures, objects, and surroundings into interlocking planes, compressing depth, and combining different visual clues in one image. Cubism did not simply turn subjects into cubes. Its central innovation was a new relationship among object, space, and picture surface: forms can be fragmented, shifted, overlapped, and still remain recognizable through carefully placed clues.

question: What does the pancreas do in digestion?
answer: In its exocrine role, the pancreas secretes digestive enzymes as pancreatic juice [5]. These include lipase, amylase and protein-cleaving enzymes such as trypsinogen, which is activated by enteropeptidase so the pancreas does not digest itself [4]. The pancreas also floods the duodenum with bicarbonate-rich fluid to neutralize acidic chyme, since the enzymes work best in a mildly alkaline environment [4]. There is no meaningful backup for pancreatic lipase, so fat digestion fails first when enzyme production falls short [3].

What Happens When Enzyme Production Falls Short Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, or EPI, is what happens when the pancreas cannot produce or deliver enough digestive enzymes to break down food properly. The causes range from loss of functional pancreatic tissue (as in chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic surgery) to conditions that block or inactivate the secretions before they reach the intestine.12PubMed Central. Causes of Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency Other Than Chronic Pancreatitis Fat digestion fails first. The reason is that your body has backup systems for protein and starch digestion: the stomach produces its own protease (pepsin), saliva contains amylase, and enzymes on the intestinal brush border finish off smaller carbohydrate chains. But there is no meaningful backup for pancreatic lipase. When pancreatic function drops below about 10% of normal, fat malabsorption becomes clinically obvious, producing pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea) and eventually causing deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins like A, D, E, and K.13PubMed. Activation of Human Pancreatic Proteolytic Enzymes: The Role of Enteropeptidase and Trypsin This tells us enteropeptidase is the true gatekeeper: without it, the whole protease cascade stalls. The system exists so the pancreas does not digest itself while still storing powerful protein-cleaving enzymes at the ready. Why Bicarbonate Is Just as Important as the Enzymes Stomach acid keeps food at a pH of roughly 1 to 3, highly acidic. Pancreatic enzymes, especially lipase and amylase, work best in a mildly alkaline environment. General relativity generalizes special relativity and refines Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation, providing a unified description of gravity as a geometric property of space and time, or four-dimensional spacetime. In particular, the curvature of spacetime is directly related to the energy, momentum, and stress of whatever is present, including matter and radiation. The relation is specified by the Einstein field equations, a system of second-order partial differential equations. question: Which direction should a ceiling fan spin in winter?

answer: One gram of fat contains 9 calories [1][2]. That is more than double the 4 calories per gram in protein and carbohydrates, which makes fat the most calorie-dense macronutrient [1]. passages.title: How Many Calories in 1 Fat Gram? The Complete Guide
passages.text: Quick answer: If you’re wondering how many calories in 1 fat gram, the number is 9 calories. That’s more than double the 4 calories per gram found in protein and carbohydrates, which is why fat is the most calorie-dense macronutrient on any nutrition label. How many calories in 1 fat gram? It’s one of the most common nutrition questions people search for, whether they’re reading a food label, building a meal plan, or trying to figure out why a “small” handful of nuts carries so many calories. passages.text: What is Moore’s Law? Exponential growth is at the heart of the rapid increase in computing capabilities. The observation that the number of transistors on computer chips doubles approximately every two years is known as Moore’s Law. Moore’s Law is not a law of nature, but an observation of a long-term trend in how technology is changing. The law was first described by Gordon E. Moore, the co-founder of Intel, in 1965.1 The chart shows Moore’s original graph that he drew in 1965 to describe this regularity. At the time, he had only a handful of data points. Note that he drew it on a logarithmic scale, and remember that a straight line on a log-axis means that the growth rate is constant, and it is therefore showing the exponential growth of the number of transistors. However, he hypothesized that this relationship would continue at a similar rate: “There is no reason to believe it will not remain constant for at least 10 years”.2 Moore’s Law has held true for more than half a century In 1965, Gordon Moore predicted that this growth would continue for another 10 years, at least. question: Who first isolated graphene, and how did they do it?
answer: Graphene was isolated in 2004 at the University of Manchester by Professor Andre Geim and Professor Kostya Novoselov [5]. They separated single-layer graphene from graphite by exfoliation, often called the scotch-tape method [5]. Their work later earned them the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics [5].

passages.text: Introduction: Why Graphene Is Called a Wonder Material Graphene is one of the most talked-about materials in modern science. It is extremely thin, strong, lightweight, flexible, and highly conductive. Because of this unusual combination, researchers and industries are exploring graphene for electronics, batteries, coatings, composites, sensors, medical devices, water filtration, construction materials, textiles, and many other applications. In simple words, graphene is a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a flat honeycomb-like pattern. The Nobel Prize describes graphene as carbon atoms joined in a flat lattice similar to a honeycomb, but only one atom thick. It also notes that graphite contains millions of graphene layers stacked on top of one another. That is what makes graphene so interesting. Carbon is already familiar to us in forms such as graphite and diamond. But when carbon atoms are arranged as a single, flat layer, they behave in extraordinary ways. Graphene can conduct electricity and heat, bend without easily breaking, remain almost transparent in thin layers, and add strength to other materials. question: When is Earth closest to the Sun, and how fast does Earth travel in its orbit?
answer: Earth is closest to the Sun at perihelion in January and farthest at aphelion in July [3]. At perihelion it is about 91 million miles (146 million km) from the Sun [1]. The sources do not say how fast Earth travels in its orbit.

passages.text: What is the jet stream? The jet stream is a core of strong winds around 5 to 7 miles above the Earth’s surface, blowing from west to east. How does the jet stream work? The jet stream flows high overhead and causes changes in the wind and pressure at that level. This affects things nearer the surface, such as areas of high and low pressure, and therefore helps shape the weather we see. Sometimes, like in a fast-moving river, the jet stream’s movement is very straight and smooth. However, its movement can buckle and loop, like a river’s meander. This will slow things up, making areas of low pressure move less predictably. The jet stream can also change the strength of an area of low pressure. It acts a bit like a vacuum cleaner, sucking air out of the top and causing it to become more intense, lowering the pressure system. The lower the pressure within a system, generally the stronger the wind, and more stormy the result. On the other hand, a slower, more buckled jet stream can cause areas of higher pressure to take charge, which typically brings less stormy weather, light winds and dry skies. What causes

What causes the jet stream? Earth is split into two hemispheres, and air is constantly moving around to spread heat and energy from the equator to the poles. Three large groups, or cells, in each hemisphere help to circulate this air within the lowest part of the atmosphere, the troposphere. Therefore, the jet stream exists largely because of a difference in heat, which in the northern hemisphere means cold air on the northern side of the jet stream and warm air to the south. The seasons also affect the position of the jet stream. In winter, there is more of a temperature difference between the equator and poles, so the jet stream is stronger and flows over the UK. This is why we tend to see wetter weather. The reverse is true in summer,where there tends to be a smaller temperature difference. question: How strong is gravity at the altitude of the International Space Station?
answer: At the ISS's height of about 400 kilometers, gravity is still about 90% of its surface value [3]. That is around 8.7 m/s² compared to 9.8 m/s² on the ground [3]. If gravity had disappeared there, the ISS would fly off in a straight line instead of orbiting [3].

passages.text: Why do astronauts float inside the ISS? Astronauts float inside the International Space Station because the station and everyone in it are constantly falling around Earth at the same speed. The result is microgravity, a condition that looks like weightlessness and changes nearly everything about life in orbit. This effect is often misunderstood as “no gravity,” but Earth’s gravity still acts strongly at ISS altitude. The interesting part is how orbital motion cancels the feeling of weight, and that difference explains both the floating and the many engineering choices inside the station. Gravity is still present at ISS altitude The International Space Station orbits roughly 400 kilometers above Earth. At that height, gravity is still about 90% as strong as it is on the surface, so astronauts are not floating because Earth’s gravity disappears. Instead, the ISS is moving fast enough to keep missing Earth as it falls. That constant forward speed, about 28,000 kilometers per hour, creates the orbital condition that makes astronauts appear weightless. What is microgravity? This is accomplished using a few different methods, including packet filtering, a proxy service, and stateful inspection. Free Firewall Assessment 2026 THREAT LANDSCAPE REPORT A firewall is a security system designed to prevent unauthorized access into or out of a computer network. Firewalls are often used to make sure internet users without access are not able to interface with private networks, or intranets, connected to the internet. A firewall is positioned between a network or a computer and a different network, like the internet. It controls the network traffic coming in and going out of the computer or network. If you do not have a firewall, virtually any data can exit your computer or network, and virtually any individual or program can come in. Firewalls protect your computer or network from unwanted traffic coming in or going out. Firewalls can also inspect and authenticate all data packets in network traffic before they are allowed to move to a more secure environment. passages.text: Self-driving cars see the road by combining cameras, lidar sensors, and radar systems that work together to build a real-time 3D map of their surroundings. Cameras capture visual details like traffic lights and lane markings. Lidar fires millions of laser pulses per second to measure exact distances. Radar uses radio waves to track objects and their speed in any weather. Software called sensor fusion merges every input into one picture the car’s brain can act on, often faster than a human can blink. passages.text: Self driving cars are moving from science fiction into everyday reality, powered by rapid advances in autonomous driving technology and sophisticated sensor systems. At the heart of these autonomous vehicles are networks of self driving car sensors that allow them to perceive the world, understand complex traffic situations, and make driving decisions in real time. What Are Self Driving Cars and Autonomous Vehicles? Self driving cars, also called autonomous vehicles, are cars capable of controlling steering, acceleration, and braking without continuous human input. These systems range from partial automation, where the driver must stay engaged, to fully autonomous operation, where the vehicle can handle all driving tasks under specific conditions. Modern autonomous vehicles rely on a combination of sensing, computing, mapping, and connectivity to operate safely. In practice, this means self driving cars use sensors, powerful onboard computers, and advanced software to interpret their surroundings and decide how to move. The Technology Stack Behind Autonomous Driving Autonomous driving technology is usually described in terms of four main functions: perception, localization, planning, and control. passages.text: Frequently Asked Questions 1. How do self driving cars handle sensor failures while driving? Self driving cars use redundant sensors so that if one fails, others can still cover the same area. If a critical fault is detected, the system typically slows down, alerts the operator, or brings the vehicle to a safe stop. 2. Do autonomous vehicles always need a high-definition map to operate? Some autonomous vehicles rely heavily on high-definition maps for precise lane-level positioning, while others focus more on real-time perception. HD maps improve comfort and robustness, but newer systems are being designed to handle more situations even when detailed maps are incomplete or outdated. 3. question: What is the difference between substitution and interstitial alloys?
answer: In a substitution alloy, atoms of the alloying agent replace atoms of the main metal, which works only when the atoms are of roughly similar size [4]. Brass is an example, with zinc atoms replacing 10–35 percent of the copper atoms [5]. In an interstitial alloy, much smaller agent atoms slip into the gaps between the main metal atoms [5]. Steel is an interstitial alloy with carbon atoms in an iron lattice [5].

passages.text: Why Do Antibiotics Stop Working Against Some Bacteria? Antibiotics stop working against some bacteria because bacterial populations can evolve traits that let them survive drugs designed to kill them or stop their growth. When an antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria are damaged or eliminated. But a few bacteria may already carry random mutations or resistance genes that protect them. Those survivors reproduce, passing their resistant traits to future generations. Over time, the population can become increasingly difficult to treat. Bacteria can resist antibiotics in several ways. Some produce enzymes that destroy the drug. Others change the molecular target the antibiotic is designed to attack, pump the drug out of the cell, reduce how much of it enters, or alter their metabolism so the drug becomes less effective. Resistance can spread unusually quickly because bacteria do not rely only on inheritance from parent cells. They can also exchange genetic material through processes known collectively as horizontal gene transfer. Resistance genes carried on mobile DNA such as plasmids can sometimes move between bacteria, even across different strains or species. passages.text: The difference between mass and weight is the mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object, while weight is a measure of the effect of gravity on that mass. Contagious yawning refers to the tendency of individuals to yawn after seeing, hearing, or even thinking about someone else yawning. answer: Impostor syndrome is a serious form of self-doubt, though it is not an official diagnosis [4]. This humorous effect is more difficult to see nowadays because the reader must be able to distinguish the two old versions of the language, but when the book was published it was much celebrated. (English translations can get some sense of the effect by having Don Quixote use the Early Modern English of the King James Bible or Shakespeare, or even Middle English.)[15][16] In Old Castilian, the letter x represented the sound written sh in modern English, so the name was originally pronounced [kiˈʃote]. question: What causes smog in cities?
answer: Smog results from a combination of pollutant emissions, atmospheric chemistry, and weather conditions [3]. Human sources include vehicles, power plants, factories, refineries, residential heating, and products that release VOCs [3]. Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and VOCs, producing ground-level ozone [1][4]. Temperature inversions in cities like Los Angeles, Beijing, and Delhi trap pollution close to the ground [2].

What is ozone? Ozone is a greenhouse gas made of three atoms of oxygen. Ozone can be helpful or harmful depending on where it is located. Stratospheric ozone, found in the upper atmosphere (which begins about 5 miles above Earth's surface), forms a protective layer that helps block ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. Because too much UV exposure can lead to vision loss and skin cancers, the global community began to phase out substances that deplete the stratospheric ozone layer when a hole appeared in 1980. Due to these efforts, the United Nations reports that the layer will likely recover by around 2066. Ground-level ozone, on the other hand, is a pollutant and a primary ingredient of smog. It forms when volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, and nitrogen oxides participate in chemical reactions in the presence of sunlight. - VOCs: Carbon-containing compounds that easily evaporate at room temperature and enter the surrounding air. question: Who invented garbage collection and why?
answer: Garbage collection was invented by American computer scientist John McCarthy around 1959 [5]. He created it to simplify manual memory management in Lisp [5]. Lisp is notable as both the first functional programming language and the first language to introduce garbage collection [4].

Or the developer might free up an object's memory space without modifying a corresponding pointer, resulting in a dangling pointer that causes the application to be buggy or even to crash. Programming languages that include garbage collection try to eliminate these types of bugs by using carefully designed GC algorithms to control memory deallocation. The garbage collector automatically detects when an object is no longer needed and removes it, freeing up the memory space allocated to that object without affecting objects that are still being used. How does garbage collection work? Each programming language implements GC differently, but they are similar in that the process occurs automatically behind the scenes. Some GC-enabled languages provide controls for launching the GC process or for optimizing its behavior, but the implementation of controls varies from one language to the next. In some cases, GC capabilities can be added to a language through a library or module. Garbage collection is a fairly common component in most modern programming languages. In general layman's terms, Garbage collection (GC) is nothing but collecting or gaining memory back which has been allocated to objects but which is not currently in use in any part of our program. Let's get into more detail. Garbage collection is the process in which programs try to free up memory space that is no longer used by objects. Garbage collection is implemented differently for every language. Most high-level programming languages have some sort of garbage collection built in. Low-level programming languages may add garbage collection through libraries. As said above, every programming language has their own way of performing GC. In C programming, developers need to take care of memory allocation and deallocation using malloc() and dealloc() functions. passages.text: What is garbage collection (GC)? Garbage collection (GC) is a memory recovery feature built into programming languages such as C# and Java. A GC-enabled programming language includes one or more garbage collectors (GC engines) that automatically free up memory space that has been allocated to objects no longer needed by the program. The reclaimed memory space can then be used for future object allocations within that program. Garbage collection ensures that a program does not exceed its memory quota or reach a point that it can no longer function. It also frees up developers from having to manually manage a program's memory, which, in turn, reduces the potential for memory-related bugs. In older programming languages, such as C and C++, the developer must manually delete objects and free up memory. Relying on manual processes made it easy to introduce bugs into the code, some of which can have serious consequences. passages.title: Garbage collection (computer science) - Wikipedia
passages.text: Garbage collection (computer science) In computer science, garbage collection (GC) is a form of automatic memory management.[2] The garbage collector attempts to reclaim memory that was allocated by the program, but is no longer referenced; such memory is called garbage. Garbage collection was invented by American computer scientist John McCarthy around 1959 to simplify manual memory management in Lisp.[3] Garbage collection relieves the programmer from doing manual memory management, where the programmer specifies what objects to de-allocate and return to the memory system and when to do so.[2] Other, similar techniques include stack allocation, region inference, and memory ownership, and combinations thereof. Garbage collection may take a significant proportion of a program's total processing time, and affect performance as a result. Resources other than memory, such as network sockets, database handles, windows, file descriptors, and device descriptors, are not typically handled by garbage collection, but rather by other methods (e.g. destructors). Some such methods de-allocate memory also. Overview [edit] Many programming languages require garbage collection, either as part of the language specification (e.g., RPL, Java, C#, D,[4] Go, and most scripting languages) or effectively for practical implementation (e.g., formal languages like lambda calculus).[5] These are said to be garbage-collected languages.

question: How often does the American Heart Association recommend aerobic and anaerobic exercise?

Crop rotation – the planned practice of growing different crops sequentially on the same piece of land – directly addresses all of these problems. Beyond restoring soil health, it cuts input costs, suppresses pests and weeds without chemicals, and creates the kind of production diversity that protects a farmer’s income when markets or weather turn unpredictable. Every crop extracts specific nutrients from the soil during its growth cycle, and planting the same species repeatedly depletes those nutrients in a highly uneven way. According to SARE (Sustainable Agriculture Research & Education), crop roots and residues improve soil fertility by stimulating microbial communities and improving soil aggregation, which in turn facilitates better water infiltration, aeration, and root growth. question: Why is the Rosetta Stone significant?
answer: The Rosetta Stone became the key to understanding Egyptian hieroglyphs [2]. It bears the same text in Greek, Egyptian Demotic and Egyptian hieroglyphics [2]. Its decoding opened Egyptian civilization to the world and led to the understanding of a long obscure dynasty [4]. Because of this, the term Rosetta Stone has come to mean a significant key to a new concept [4].

Red Blood Cells: Built for Gas Transport Red blood cells, or erythrocytes, are the most abundant formed elements in blood and are specialized for one major task: transporting respiratory gases. Their main job is to carry oxygen from the lungs to body tissues and help return carbon dioxide from tissues to the lungs for exhalation. This function may sound simple, but it is essential for every cell that depends on aerobic metabolism. Without enough functional erythrocytes, even tissues with healthy blood vessels and working mitochondria cannot receive the oxygen they need. The structure of an erythrocyte matches its job. passages.title: How Does Blood Carry Oxygen Around the Body?
passages.text: reaches tissues where oxygen levels are lower, hemoglobin releases some of its oxygen. The oxygen then diffuses out of the blood and into nearby cells. This arrangement is important: hemoglobin does not simply hold oxygen permanently. It acts as a reversible carrier, loading oxygen where it is abundant and unloading it where it is needed. How blood delivers oxygen to tissues After leaving the heart, oxygen-rich blood travels through progressively smaller blood vessels: arteries, arterioles, and finally capillaries. Capillaries are narrow vessels with walls only one cell thick. Their structure allows oxygen to move efficiently from the blood into surrounding tissues. Cells continually use oxygen for cellular respiration, a set of chemical reactions that produces usable energy for the body’s activities. As cells consume oxygen, the oxygen concentration around them falls. This helps maintain the gradient that drives oxygen out of the blood and into the tissues. question: Why does salt preserve meat?
answer: Salt preserves food by drawing out water and by inhibiting the growth of bacteria [2]. Its ability to inhibit bacterial growth is what prevents salted meat from spoiling [5]. During salt curing, letting moisture escape through air circulation also helps prevent the growth of bacteria [4].

question: What is the climate of the Sahel like?
answer: The Sahel has a tropical climate with very hot summers, when mean maximum temperatures range from 33°C to 36°C [2]. Rainfall averages about 600mm per year in the southern zone but only 200mm in the north [2]. A rainy season lasts from May to September, followed by a dry season of six to eight months [2].

question: Why did the Western Roman Empire fall?

passages.text: What's the difference between a heart attack and a cardiac arrest? A heart attack and a cardiac arrest are not the same condition. A heart attack happens when there is a sudden loss of blood flow to a part of the heart muscle, while a cardiac arrest is when your heart suddenly stops pumping blood around your body. A cardiac arrest is an electrical issue with the heart and the person affected will be unconscious, and a heart attack is a circulatory issue where the person is likely to be conscious. Is it a heart attack or a cardiac arrest? A heart attack happens when the blood supply to the heart muscle is cut off. This is often caused by a blood clot in one of the coronary arteries. The heart is still pumping blood around the body during a heart attack. The person will usually be conscious and breathing. A sudden cardiac arrest is when your heart stops pumping blood around your body. It occurs when your heart's electrical system does not work properly and your heart starts beating too quickly, too slowly or irregularly. This is an abnormal heart rhythm, called an arrhythmia. The empirical principle is usually known as the Pareto principle.[19] With regard to variation causality, this principle states that there is a non-random distribution of the slopes of the numerous (theoretically infinite) terms in the general equation. All of the terms are independent of each other by definition. Interdependent factors appear as multiplication terms. The Pareto principle states that the effect of the dominant term is much greater than the second-largest effect term, which in turn is much greater than the third, and so on.[20] There is no explanation for this phenomenon; that is why we refer to it as an empirical principle. The mathematical logic is known as the square-root-of-the-sum-of-the-squares axiom. This states that the variation caused by the steepest slope must be squared, and then the result added to the square of the variation caused by the second-steepest slope, and so on. The total observed variation is then the square root of the total sum of the variation caused by individual slopes squared. This derives from the probability density function for multiple variables or the multivariate distribution (we are treating each term as an independent variable). Peer pressure typically begins around age 10 and intensifies through junior high and high school. As children become more independent from parents during early adolescence, friends and classmates take on a larger role in shaping choices, which increases both the frequency and the intensity of peer influence. Is peer pressure always negative? No. Peer pressure can be positive when friends encourage healthy behavior such as studying, exercising, or volunteering. Research shows most teens report their friends do not pressure them toward risky behavior. Direct peer pressure is an explicit request or dare to act now, such as being offered a substance. passages.title: How Does a Toilet Work? The Flush Cycle and Its Parts
passages.text: How Does a Toilet Work? The Flush Cycle and Its Parts A standard toilet works by dumping a tank of stored water into the bowl fast enough to start a siphon, which pulls the bowl’s contents through a curved trapway and into the drain, and then automatically refilling both tank and bowl for the next use. Gravity does nearly all the work; the only moving parts are a handle, a chain, a rubber flapper and a float-controlled fill valve. Knowing how does a toilet work at that level is surprisingly useful, because almost every common toilet complaint, from a constantly running tank to a weak flush or a puddle at the base, traces back to one specific part. This guide walks through the flush cycle step by step, explains each part in a reference table, compares gravity, pressure-assisted and dual-flush designs, covers water use standards, maps typical problems to their causes, lists typical repair cost ranges and describes what a home inspector checks. How Does a Toilet Work? The Flush Cycle and Its Parts A standard toilet works by dumping a tank of stored water into the bowl fast enough to start a siphon, which pulls the bowl’s contents through a curved trapway and into the drain, and then automatically refilling both tank and bowl for the next use. Gravity does nearly all the work; the only moving parts are a handle, a chain, a rubber flapper and a float-controlled fill valve. Knowing how does a toilet work at that level is surprisingly useful, because almost every common toilet complaint, from a constantly running tank to a weak flush or a puddle at the base, traces back to one specific part. This guide walks through the flush cycle step by step, explains each part in a reference table, compares gravity, pressure-assisted and dual-flush designs, covers water use standards, maps typical problems to their causes, lists typical repair cost ranges and describes what a home inspector checks. question: What heights have different surveys given for Mount Everest?
answer: In 1856 Andrew Waugh announced Everest as 8,840 m (29,002 ft) based on the Great Trigonometrical Survey [5]. From 1952 to 1954 the Survey of India measured 8,847.73 m, and a 1975 Chinese measurement gave 8,848.13 m [5]. A joint 2020 survey by Nepal and China set the height at 8,848.86 m [3].

passages.title: How Was Mount Everest Measured? And by Whom?
passages.text: Everest is the highest mountain in the world. But it isn’t next to the sea, so how was the measurement of 29,031 feet (8,848m) above sea level arrived at? And who first measured Mount Everest, and why? Mount Everest was measured using imaginary triangles and basic mathematics. Everest was measured by British surveyors, who figured out how high it was in 1854. The story of the Great Trigonometrical Survey started with tigers, camels, lost villages, elephants, goats, telescopes and surveying instruments. It ended with the discovery of the highest point on the earth’s surface. When the British got round to surveying the Himalayas they finally discovered Everest. It was a huge mountain hiding at the back that, when measured, proved to be higher than any other mountain in the world. But how did they know it was the highest mountain? You could hardly dangle a ruler down the side of Everest. So how was it done? The British in India decided to survey the land they had colonised, so they commissioned a Great Trigonometrical Survey in 1802. Imaginary triangles were to be drawn all over India, starting at the southern end and eventually reaching the Himalayas over 1,500 miles away.

passages.text: Mount Everest Mount Everest (known in Nepali as Sagarmāthā[a], in Sherpa as Chamolangma[4], and in Tibetan as Jomolangma/Čhomolangma[b]) is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level. It lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas and marks part of the China–Nepal border at its summit.[5] Its height was most recently measured in 2020 through a joint survey by Nepalese and Chinese authorities as 8,848.86 m (29,031 ft 8+1⁄2 in).[6][7] Mount Everest attracts many climbers, including highly experienced mountaineers. There are two main climbing routes, one approaching the summit from the southeast in Nepal (known as the standard route) and the other from the north in China. While not posing substantial technical climbing challenges on the standard route, Everest presents dangers such as altitude sickness, weather, and wind, as well as hazards from avalanches and the Khumbu Icefall. As of May 2024, 340 people have died on Everest. Over 200 bodies remain on the mountain and have not been removed due to the dangerous conditions.[8][9] Climbers typically ascend only part of Mount Everest's elevation, as the mountain's full elevation is measured from the geoid, which approximates sea level. passages.text: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. History of the Discovery and Understanding of Acid Rain Scientific recognition of acid rain developed gradually over more than a century. What began as local observations of polluted city air evolved into an international environmental issue involving atmospheric transport, ecosystem damage, and cross-border policy agreements. Early Observations In 1852, Scottish chemist Robert Angus Smith first described “acid rain” while studying air pollution in industrial Manchester, England. He linked coal burning to acidic precipitation and environmental damage. Mid-20th Century Recognition In the 1950s–1970s, scientists in Scandinavia and North America documented declining fish populations and forest damage. They discovered that sulfur emissions from industrial regions could travel hundreds or thousands of kilometers before falling as acid deposition. Policy Response In the United States, the Clean Air Act and its 1990 amendments established emissions trading programs to reduce SO₂ and NOₓ. Similar agreements were implemented in Europe. passages.text: What is Acid Rain? Acid rain, or acid deposition, is a broad term that includes any form of precipitation with acidic components, such as sulfuric or nitric acid that fall to the ground from the atmosphere in wet or dry forms. This can include rain, snow, fog, hail or even dust that is acidic. What Causes Acid Rain? Acid rain results when sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOX) are emitted into the atmosphere and transported by wind and air currents. The SO2 and NOX react with water, oxygen and other chemicals to form sulfuric and nitric acids. These then mix with water and other materials before falling to the ground. While a small portion of the SO2 and NOX that cause acid rain is from natural sources such as volcanoes, most of it comes from the burning of fossil fuels. The major sources of SO2 and NOX in the atmosphere are: - Burning of fossil fuels to generate electricity. Two thirds of SO2 and one fourth of NOX in the atmosphere come from electric power generators. - Vehicles and heavy equipment. - Manufacturing, oil refineries and other industries. Buffering Capacity Many forests, streams, and lakes that experience acid rain don’t suffer effects because the soil in those areas can buffer the acid rain by neutralizing the acidity in the rainwater flowing through it. This capacity depends on the thickness and composition of the soil and the type of bedrock underneath it. In areas such as mountainous parts of the Northeast United States, the soil is thin and lacks the ability to adequately neutralize the acid in the rain water. As a result, these areas are particularly vulnerable and the acid and aluminum can accumulate in the soil, streams, or lakes. Episodic Acidification Melting snow and heavy rain downpours can result in what is known as episodic acidification. Lakes that do not normally have a high level of acidity may temporarily experience effects of acid rain when the melting snow or downpour brings greater amounts of acidic deposition and the soil can’t buffer it. Sometimes it projects from a vertical surface such as a wall. A cantilever can be in the form of a beam, plate, truss, or slab. When subjected to a structural load at its far, unsupported end, the cantilever carries the load to the support where it applies a shear stress and a bending moment.[1] Cantilever construction allows overhanging structures without external support. In bridges, railroad crossings, towers, and buildings [edit] Cantilevers are widely found in construction, notably in cantilever bridges and balconies (see corbel). For your furry predecessors, this response served two crucial functions that helped them survive in harsh environments. Contraction of arrector pili muscles have a principal function in the majority of mammals of providing thermal insulation. passages.text: Why We Get Goosebumps Chances are you’ve experienced the phenomenon of goosebumps. Maybe you were moved by a beautiful song or felt an intense rush of emotions. Or perhaps you were just cold. Goosebumps may seem like a shared human experience, but not everyone gets them and not everyone gets them under the same circumstances. “Whether one gets goosebumps varies widely from person to person,” says Jon McPhetres, PhD, a biological psychologist based in Durham, United Kingdom, who has extensively studied goosebumps. What Are Goosebumps? What Causes Goosebumps? “Much of your body uses the same wiring — the sympathetic nervous system, or SNS — that is connected to your goosebump muscles, called the arrector pili,” Dr. McPhetres says. Any time the SNS is activated, you might also experience goosebumps. They're called goosebumps, and they're usually not a big deal. But sometimes they're caused by a medical condition that needs treatment. The reason goosebumps show up has to do with a tiny muscle that surrounds the root of every hair on your body. When the muscle tightens, a small bump appears on your skin. Cold If you get too cold, your brain alerts your body that it should take steps to warm up. Goosebumps are one of those signals. They're also an attempt to trap warm air next to your skin and let you hold on to your body heat. If you have goosebumps because you're cold, other signs can include: - Shivers - An urge to hug yourself - Pale skin Once you warm up, your goosebumps should go away. passages.text: How Do Seeds Know When It Is the Right Time to Sprout? Seeds do not consciously "know" when to sprout. Instead, they contain biological mechanisms that respond to environmental conditions such as moisture, temperature, oxygen and, in some species, light. These signals interact with the seed's internal chemistry to determine whether dormancy should continue or germination should begin. Water is usually the crucial first trigger because a dry seed has very little metabolic activity. After absorbing water, enzymes and cellular processes become active, stored food reserves become available, and the embryo can resume growth. Plant hormones—especially abscisic acid and gibberellins—help regulate the balance between remaining dormant and germinating. These mechanisms prevent many seeds from sprouting during conditions in which a young seedling would have little chance of survival. How did the seed know it was time? It didn't know in the conscious sense. A seed has no brain. No eyes. No nervous system. Instead, evolution has equipped seeds with sophisticated biological mechanisms capable of responding to their environment. They can detect conditions associated with: water; temperature; oxygen; light; seasonal change. Inside the seed, hormones and genes process those environmental signals chemically. If the conditions satisfy the biological requirements of that particular species, dormancy weakens and germination begins. If conditions remain unsuitable, many seeds simply wait. A seed does not predict the future—it uses environmental signals to estimate whether the present offers a good opportunity to survive. question: What was the Magna Carta?
answer: The Magna Carta, Latin for "Great Charter", was the document setting out what King John and the barons agreed [2]. It had 63 clauses with rules on land ownership, taxation and people's legal rights [2]. It stated that the monarch was not above the law, that everyone had the right to a fair trial, and that the king could not raise new taxes without the barons' agreement [2]. King John sealed it on 15 June 1215 [2][4].

question: What is CAM photosynthesis in cacti?
answer: CAM, or Crassulacean Acid Metabolism, is a water-saving process in which a cactus opens its stomata at night instead of during the day [4]. This reduces water loss in desert environments [4].

Law of Supply and Demand Definition The law of supply and demand states that if a product has a high demand and low supply, the price will increase. Conversely, if there is low demand and high supply, the price will decrease. Market equilibrium occurs when demand and supply intersect to create a stable price. When figuring out your monthly budget, microeconomic theory plays a part whether or not you’re familiar with this concept. The law of supply and demand can be particularly useful to individuals who want to make smart buying and selling decisions. This fundamental economic concept can be tricky, but, once understood, can be easily applied to your money management decisions, especially when buying consumer goods. passages.title: How Do Glaciers Carve Valleys? Mystery Solved - Live Science
passages.text: How Do Glaciers Carve Valleys? Mystery Solved Since the dawn of time, humans have wondered how mountains and valleys came to be. Now, a new research technique has uncovered the specifics of the million-year process by which glaciers carve valleys in the landscape. Glacial valleys, such as Yosemite Valley in California and the Fiordland in the Southern Alps of New Zealand, are always U-shaped, and are surrounded on all sides by high mountain ridges. It was known previously that these low-relief areas were drudged out by enormous, slow-moving glaciers . But for the first time, geologists at the University of California at Berkeley led by David Shuster have discovered why the formations look the way they do. Shuster developed a method (called helium-4/helium-3 thermochronometry) that reveals how rocks in the Fiordland gradually worked their way up to the surface. The method pinpoints the temperature of minerals in the rock at different times in their geologic history, and because temperature increases with a rock's depth, the temperature history of the mineral is tied to how deeply it was buried over the past few million years. passages.title: U-Shaped Valleys, Fjords, and Hanging Valleys - U.S. National ...
passages.text: Glaciers carve a set of distinctive, steep-walled, flat-bottomed valleys. U-shaped valleys, fjords, and hanging valleys are examples of the kinds of valleys glaciers can erode. U-Shaped Valleys Valley glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, as opposed to the V-shaped valleys carved by rivers. During periods when Earth’s climate cools, glaciers form and begin to flow downslope. Often, they take the easiest path, occupying the low V-shaped valleys once carved by rivers. As glaciers flow through these valleys, they concentrate erosive action over the entire valley, widening its floor and over-steepening its walls. After the glacier retreats, it leaves behind a flat-bottomed, steep-walled U-shaped valley. Fjords Valley glaciers sometimes flow through narrow inlets (fjords) into the ocean. They over-steepen the walls around them, as they do when carving u-shaped valleys. Thus, fjords have tall, steep walls like glacial valleys, but their floors are below sea level and thus are inundated with ocean water. Hanging Valleys A small mountain glacier may join a larger valley glacier, just as a stream may join a larger river. question: How many time zones does Russia have?
answer: Russia has 11 time zones [2][3]. They run from Kaliningrad Time (UTC+2) on the Baltic coast to Kamchatka Time (UTC+12) on the Pacific, a spread of ten hours [4]. This count has been in place since October 26, 2014, after a brief consolidation to nine zones between 2010 and 2014 was reversed [4].

passages.text: Last reviewed on August 28, 2026 How many time zones does Russia have? Russia has 11 time zones, more than any other country in the world. They run from Kaliningrad Time (UTC+2) on the Baltic coast to Kamchatka Time (UTC+12) on the Pacific, a spread of ten hours across a single country. When it is 9:00 a.m. in Kaliningrad, it is already 7:00 p.m. in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky. The current count has been in place since October 26, 2014. Between 2010 and 2014 Russia briefly consolidated to nine zones, but the change pushed several regions too far from solar time and was reversed. Since 2014 none of the Russian time zones change for daylight saving, so every offset on this page is valid all year. The full story is on our daylight saving time in Russia page. question: What is the difference between a meteor and a meteorite?
answer: A meteor is the streak of light seen when a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere and burns up, often called a shooting star [2]. A meteorite is what remains when a meteoroid survives the trip through the atmosphere and hits the ground [1]. Usually only about five percent of the original meteoroid survives to reach Earth [5]. Meteors are found in the atmosphere, while meteorites are found on Earth's surface [4].

question: Does heavy water ice float in ordinary water?
answer: Heavy water ice sinks in ordinary water [2]. The extra mass from deuterium makes heavy water ice denser than ordinary liquid water [2]. However, heavy water ice floats in liquid heavy water, because solid D₂O is still less dense than liquid D₂O [2].

passages.text: Why does ice float? Why does ice float in water, instead of sinking to the bottom? It has to do with water's density and molecular structure. Whether it's the cubes in your cocktail or a raft for Arctic seals, floating ice is a basic fact of nature we may take for granted. Floating ice is "such a fundamental fact of the world, it's hard to truly imagine what the world would be like [without it]," said Brent Minchew, an associate professor of geophysics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. But did you ever stop to think why ice floats on water, instead of sinking to the bottom? It has to do with the density of water. Water ice, the solid state of water, floats because it is less dense than its liquid form. Most other substances, by contrast, become denser in the solid phase. Ice made from heavy water does not float in ordinary water. Heavy water is deuterium oxide, D₂O, rather than ordinary water, H₂O. Each deuterium atom contains a proton and a neutron, so D₂O has more mass than H₂O. Heavy water ice still forms an open ice-like crystal structure, but the extra mass from deuterium makes it denser than ordinary liquid water. Heavy water has a density around 1.105 g/mL, compared with about 0.998 g/mL for ordinary water near room temperature. So: - Ordinary ice floats in ordinary water. - Heavy water ice sinks in ordinary water. - Heavy water ice floats in liquid heavy water, because solid D₂O is still less dense than liquid D₂O, much as ordinary ice is less dense than ordinary liquid water. This distinction gives students a useful reminder: floating depends on the density of the object compared with the density of the liquid, not simply on whether the substance is “ice.” Why Floating Ice Matters Floating ice is not just a curiosity, it is essential for life:

passages.title: Why does ice float on water? - BBC Science Focus Magazine
passages.text: Perhaps a cold, refreshing drink on a hot day wouldn't look so appealing if the ice cubes dropped like a stone to the bottom of the glass. But why does ice float on water? In fact, why does anything float at all? What makes something float? An object less dense than water will float. We can explain this phenomenon with the help of a theory called Archimedes' principle. Before you carry on, we should warn you: the following explanation will contain a lot of maths. When you place an object in a glass of water,it will feel a buoyant force that pushes it upwards against gravity. For the object to be fully or partially underwater, some of the water must have been displaced - which you can see in the rising water level. Archimedes' principle says that the upward buoyant force pushing against the submerged object is equal to the weight of the displaced water. An object's weight is equal to its mass multiplied by g, the acceleration due to gravity. So, the upward buoyant force – let's call it FB, for buoyant – is equal to mass of water x g. Density is mass divided by volume, which we

passages.title: Why Does Ice Float on Water - Science Facts
passages.text: of neighboring water molecules, giving rise to weak hydrogen bonds between them. In the liquid state, all the water molecules are loosely held together and are free to move. On cooling, the molecules try to come closer, increasing the density. But once the temperature drops below 4oC, the repelling nature of negative oxygen atoms of the neighboring molecules prevent them from coming any closer. That is when its density starts to fall. As it reaches the solid state (ice), the hydrogen bonds become stable and arrange themselves in such a way that the adjacent oxygen atoms are spread far apart from each other, leaving a lot of space between the molecules. This causes ice to have a higher volume and lesser density than water, making it float. FAQs 1. Why does ice sink in alcohol? – Alcohol has a lower density than ice, which makes it sink. 2. Does heavy water ice float or sink in ordinary water? – Heavy water ice sinks in regular water as it has a higher density (but it will float in heavy water). question: Why does soap work poorly in hard water?
answer: Hard water contains relatively high concentrations of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions [2]. These ions react with ordinary soap to form poorly soluble compounds known as soap scum, which reduces the soap available to remove grease [2]. This explains why soap may produce less lather and leave deposits in hard water [2].

Why soap sometimes works poorly in hard water Hard water contains relatively high concentrations of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. These ions can react with ordinary soap to form poorly soluble compounds commonly known as soap scum. When this happens, some of the soap is converted into material that does not remain usefully dissolved in the water. The resulting deposits may accumulate on sinks, bathtubs, fabrics, and skin. They can also reduce the amount of soap available to help remove grease. This explains why soap may produce less lather and leave deposits in hard water. Lather is not a perfect measure of cleaning performance, but the chemical reaction that produces soap scum can genuinely interfere with cleaning. Many modern laundry detergents and dishwashing products use synthetic surfactants that are less susceptible to this problem. They can continue to function in hard water without forming the same insoluble deposits as traditional soap. passages.text: Soap removes dirt and grease by helping water loosen and carry away substances that water cannot easily remove on its own. The secret lies in the molecular structure of soap: each soap molecule has one end that mixes readily with water and another that attaches to oils and grease. This dual nature allows soap to surround greasy particles, lift them from surfaces, and help wash them away when rinsed with water. The process involves several related actions, including reducing water’s surface tension, loosening dirt, forming tiny structures called micelles, and suspending oily material in water. Together, these actions make soap an effective cleaning agent for skin, clothing, dishes, and many other surfaces. Why water alone cannot remove all dirt and grease Water is excellent at dissolving many substances, including salt, sugar, and some other water-soluble materials. However, it does not dissolve grease and most oils effectively. The reason comes down to the molecular properties of these substances. Water molecules are polar, meaning their electrical charge is distributed unevenly. This allows them to interact strongly with other polar substances and with many ions. Oils and grease, by contrast, consist mainly of nonpolar molecules that do not interact favorably with water. As

The surface matters too, because grease may cling differently to smooth glass, textured plastic, fabric fibers, or skin. The amount and type of soap influence how much surfactant is available to interact with the contaminants. Water hardness can reduce the effectiveness of traditional soap, while temperature can change how easily grease moves. Rubbing, brushing, stirring, and flowing water provide physical forces that help detach and transport dirt. Time also plays a role. Allowing a cleaning solution to contact a surface can help it penetrate or loosen certain residues, although longer contact is not always better and may be unsuitable for delicate materials. The key is the combined effect of these factors. Soap makes grease and dirt easier for water to remove, but successful cleaning still depends on loosening the contaminants and rinsing them away. At the molecular level, soap bridges the gap between water and oily substances. At the everyday level, that chemistry makes it possible to wash greasy dishes, clean dirty hands, and remove many kinds of residue from surfaces that water alone cannot clean effectively.

Why rinsing removes the dirt Loosening grease is only part of cleaning. The contaminants must also be carried away. After soap has helped detach dirt and disperse grease, rinsing introduces fresh water that transports the suspended material off the surface. Because the soap molecules help keep oily substances dispersed, the grease is less likely to immediately collect back into a single mass or reattach to the surface. Flowing water dilutes and carries away the cleaning solution, along with the dirt and oil it contains. On skin, the process removes much of the loosened material from the outer surface. On dishes, it carries away food residue and grease. In laundry, water movement through the fabric helps remove dirt that the detergent has loosened and dispersed. Rinsing matters because cleaning does not necessarily mean that contaminants have been chemically destroyed. In most ordinary washing, the grease and dirt are physically removed from the item and carried away in the wastewater. passages.text: What a CT Scan Shows, and Why Doctors Order One Key Takeaways - A CT scan reconstructs hundreds of X-ray measurements into cross-sectional slices, showing bone, organs, blood vessels and fresh bleeding in detail that a single X-ray cannot. - The most common reason for an urgent CT is to rule dangerous conditions such as brain bleeding, lung clots, aortic tears or a perforated organ in or out within minutes. - Head CT can show a bleed within minutes of a stroke, but a blockage-type stroke may be invisible in its first hours, so a normal scan means no bleed was seen, not that the brain is fine. - Harvard Health estimates a chest CT at about 7 millisieverts and an abdominal CT at about 8, compared with roughly 3 millisieverts of natural background radiation per year. - CT shows structure rather than function, so nerve problems, early cartilage damage, seizures, migraine and most blood cancers are not detected by it and need other tests. - No major guideline body recommends whole-body CT screening for healthy adults because it finds many harmless incidental lesions that lead to further tests without proven benefit. What CT Scans Reveal That X-Rays Can’t Soft Tissue and Organ Detail X-rays do not clearly show soft tissues like muscles, ligaments or internal organs. A CT scan can visualize the brain, lungs, liver, kidneys and intestines with precision. For instance, if a patient has abdominal pain, a CT scan can identify appendicitis, intestinal blockage or internal bleeding that an X-ray might completely miss. Subtle Bone and Joint Injuries While X-rays are good for spotting fractures, small or complex breaks in the spine, skull or joints can go undetected. A CT scan provides a more detailed view of the bone’s structure and can detect hairline fractures or joint damage that could lead to long-term complications if left untreated. Internal Bleeding and Blood Vessel Problems CT angiography, a special type of CT scan, can highlight blood vessels and detect blockages, clots or aneurysms. X-rays cannot show blood flow or the interior of vessels, making CT scans essential for diagnosing circulation-related issues. passages.title: What Can Chest CT Scans Show That X-Rays Can’t?
passages.text: You go in with a cough. The doctor orders a chest X-ray. It comes back “clear.” You’re relieved—until the symptoms stick around. Sound familiar? X-rays have been a go-to diagnostic tool for decades. And they’re great—for some things. But when it comes to catching serious conditions early, a chest CT scan can reveal what an X-ray simply can’t. At Life Guard Imaging in Tampa, we offer low-dose CT chest scans designed specifically for preventative care—to give you answers before a problem becomes a diagnosis. What’s the Difference Between an X-Ray and a CT Scan? There is a huge difference between an X-ray and a CT scan—and it all comes down to two important terms: clarity and detail. Here’s a quick comparison: - X-rays are two-dimensional.They show shadows of bones and organs. - CT scans are three-dimensional.They capture hundreds of detailed cross-sections of your chest, creating a crystal-clear image of what’s happening inside. It’s a lot like comparing a snapshot to a 4K video. Both are useful—but one offers a whole lot more. CT cannot show how organs function, so conditions such as epilepsy, migraine, irregular heart rhythms and most nerve problems are invisible to it. It also sees cartilage, ligaments, spinal discs and the spinal cord poorly compared with MRI, can miss very small or flat tumors, and may not show a blockage-type stroke in its first hours. A normal CT excludes what was looked for, not everything. What is the most common reason for a CT scan? Ruling out something dangerous quickly is the most common reason, particularly in emergency care: head injury, suspected stroke, chest pain that might be a clot or aortic tear, and severe abdominal pain. Outside emergencies, CT is widely used to find the cause of symptoms, stage and monitor cancer, plan surgery or radiotherapy, and guide biopsy needles to the right spot. What cancers show up on a CT scan? Most solid tumors large enough to distort tissue can be seen, including lung, liver, kidney, pancreatic, adrenal, ovarian and many bowel and lymph node cancers, along with spread to the liver, lungs and bones. question: What is two-factor authentication and why is it safer?
answer: Two-factor authentication is a security process that requires users to verify their identity with two separate types of authentication factors, usually a password and something else the user has access to [3]. An example is signing in with a password and then confirming a code sent to your phone [1]. It reduces the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised [1]. It also protects against threats like credential theft, phishing and brute-force attacks [1].

passages.text: Most internet users are familiar with the idea of using 2FA online. Most digital services use two-factor authentication to protect online accounts, and as such, users may encounter 2FA for email accounts, banking portals, and social media profiles. But what is 2FA, and how does it work? And, perhaps more importantly, what are the 2FA benefits for users? What is 2FA? 2FA is a security process that requires users to verify their identities with two separate types of authentication factors. This is usually a password and something else the user has access to. Also known as two-step verification or dual-factor authentication, the system offers additional security to protect users’ credentials and minimizes the risk of unauthorized users accessing accounts. For this reason, using 2FA online is becoming increasingly common. How does two-factor authentication work? In general, using 2FA online is a multi-step process. Two-factor authentication is a security process that requires users to verify their identity with two separate types of authentication factors, usually a password and something else the user has access to [3]. A WAF can help identify and block certain malicious requests, including common web attacks such as: - SQL injection - Cross-site scripting (XSS) - Malicious HTTP requests A WAF can be deployed in front of a web application, on a server, or through a cloud-based service. OWASP notes that WAFs are designed to protect web applications and can inspect HTTP traffic for common application-layer attacks. A network firewall and a WAF are not the same thing. A network firewall controls network traffic between systems or networks, while a WAF focuses specifically on protecting web applications. How does a network firewall work? question: What are GMO crops and how are they made?
answer: Genetic modification of crops involves adding a specific stretch of DNA into the plant's genome, giving it new or different characteristics [4]. To produce a GM plant, new DNA is transferred into plant cells, which are usually grown in tissue culture where they develop into plants [4]. The seeds produced by these plants inherit the new DNA [4]. GMO crops grown in the United States include soybeans, corn, sugar beets, canola and cotton [3].

passages.title: How Does Freeze Drying Work?– Harvest Right
passages.text: Freeze drying makes it possible to preserve an incredibly wide variety of foods while maintaining much of their nutritional value, flavor, color, and structure. But how does freeze dryting actually work? Freeze drying removes water from frozen food through a process called sublimation. Instead of allowing frozen water inside the food to melt into liquid, a freeze dryer creates conditions that allow ice to change directly from a solid into water vapor. The process has three main stages: - Freezing — Water inside the food freezes into ice. - Primary drying — A vacuum and controlled heat allow the ice to sublimate into water vapor. - Secondary drying — Additional moisture remaining in the food is removed. The result is food with very little moisture remaining. Because much of the food's physical structure remains after the water is removed, many freeze-dried foods are lightweight, porous, and easy to rehydrate. Removing moisture also makes it possible to store freeze-dried food without continuous refrigeration. When food is completely freeze dried, appropriately packaged, and stored under suitable conditions, many foods can last for years, with some lasting up to 25 years. No. Freeze drying should not be considered a method for killing bacteria or sterilizing food. Safe food handling still matters. Does freeze drying remove nutrients? Freeze drying can preserve nearly all of the nutritional value of many foods. Exact nutrient retention varies depending on the food, nutrient, processing, packaging, and storage conditions. How long does freeze-dried food last? When food is completely freeze dried, appropriately packaged, and stored under suitable conditions, many foods can last for years, with some lasting up to 25 years. Why is freeze-dried food so light? A significant portion of the weight of many foods comes from water. Removing most of that water dramatically reduces the food's weight. Can freeze-dried food absorb moisture again? Yes. Freeze-dried food can absorb moisture from its environment, which is why appropriate packaging is important after drying. What foods can I freeze dry? You can freeze dry a wide variety of fruits, vegetables, meats, dairy products, eggs, complete meals, leftovers, snacks, desserts, and other foods. Foods that are almost entirely fat or oil generally don't freeze dry well.

passages.text: Food? Moisture plays a major role in food spoilage. Bacteria, mold, and yeast need available moisture to grow, and water also contributes to chemical and enzymatic reactions that can affect food quality over time. Freeze drying removes most of that moisture, helping slow microbial growth and many of the changes that cause food to deteriorate. Once the food is freeze dried, appropriate packaging helps prevent moisture from returning and limits exposure to oxygen. This combination is what makes long-term shelf-stable storage possible. Does Freeze Drying Kill Bacteria? No. Freeze drying is a preservation process, not a sterilization process. Microorganisms can survive freeze drying. That's why safe food selection, sanitation, preparation, cooking when required, complete drying, packaging, and safe handling still matter. passages.title: How Does an MRI Machine Use Magnets to Create Medical Images?
passages.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses powerful magnets, radio waves, and computer processing to create detailed pictures of structures inside the human body. Unlike X-rays and computed tomography (CT) scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation. Instead, it takes advantage of the magnetic properties of hydrogen atoms, which are abundant in water and fat throughout the body. The central magnet inside an MRI machine creates a strong, stable magnetic field that influences the behavior of hydrogen nuclei in the body. Radio waves briefly disturb their alignment, and specialized receiver coils detect the signals they produce as they return toward their original state. A computer then processes these signals to construct detailed images of organs, muscles, bones, blood vessels, and other tissues. Understanding this process requires looking at how magnets interact with the body, how hydrogen atoms generate detectable signals, and how an MRI scanner turns those signals into medical images. Why MRI machines use powerful magnets The human body contains large amounts of hydrogen because water and many biological molecules contain hydrogen atoms. It describes how quickly the hydrogen nuclei lose their coordinated motion in the plane perpendicular to the main magnetic field. Although the nuclei initially precess in a relatively coordinated way after a radiofrequency pulse, their magnetic interactions with one another and small variations in their local magnetic environments cause them to gradually lose synchronization. As this coordination decreases, the detectable signal becomes weaker. T1 and T2 relaxation provide different kinds of information about tissue composition and molecular surroundings. MRI scanners use these differences to create images with varying contrast. A third concept, called T2-star (T2*), describes signal loss caused by both interactions between nuclei and variations in the magnetic field. These variations can result from imperfections in the scanner’s magnetic field or differences in the magnetic properties of nearby tissues. Together, these relaxation processes explain why different tissues produce different signal patterns even when they contain similar amounts of hydrogen. question: What is an alloy and why are alloys used?
answer: An alloy is a material made by mixing two or more metals, sometimes with non-metal elements like carbon [3]. Alloys are created to enhance the properties of the metals they contain [1]. They can be stronger, harder or more corrosion-resistant than pure metals [3]. Because of this they are widely used in construction, manufacturing, electronics and automotive industries [3].

question: What is the Dunning-Kruger effect?
answer: The Dunning-Kruger effect happens when someone who is not especially knowledgeable in an area overestimates how much they know or how good they are at an activity [3]. It is a type of cognitive bias [3]. It was named after Cornell University psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger, who coined the term in a 1999 paper [3].

passages.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect: Causes, Examples, and Impact - WebMD
passages.text: Is the Dunning-Kruger effect real? Since Cornell University researchers first named it in 1999, numerous other studies have looked at the concept. Some have cast doubt on the concept, or suggested it's not as big as reported. But studies have found the Dunning-Kruger effect in many areas: among medical students, college students, and in attitudes about politics and health.Â What are the four stages of the Dunning-Kruger effect? The four stages describe not the effect itself, but four stages of learning any skill or new information. They are:Â - Unconscious incompetence, when you don't know what you don't knowÂ - Conscious incompetence, when you're aware of what you don't know but haven't yet learned itÂ - Conscious competence, when you're gaining knowledgeÂ - Unconscious competence, when you've mastered somethingÂ Is the Dunning-Kruger effect good or bad? If you overestimate your knowledge and abilities, you may run into problems at work or school. The Dunning-Kruger effect can also affect your health, politics, and relationships with others.Â

answer: Garúa fog occurs near the coast of Chile and Peru when sea fog travels inland and suddenly meets hot air [5]. The fog droplets shrink by evaporation, producing a nearly invisible transparent mist that still makes drivers use windshield wipers [5].

passages.text: What causes fog to form, how it fades away and why it can linger for so long TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - While fog is possible any time of year that conditions are right, there is a “fog season” here in NW Ohio and SE Michigan. It’s most common from October through March and sometimes into April, but fall fog has different mechanisms from the fog we usually get during the winter and early spring. There are many different types of fog, but during the autumn it’s typically radiation fog. For that you need clear skies because that’s what allows heat at the Earth’s surface to “radiate” out into space, hence the name. As temps at the surface drop close to the dewpoint, it helps to have a little moisture in the ground to saturate the air and facilitate fog formation. Lastly, very light or calm winds are needed because any gusts over 10 mph can quickly dissipate a bank of fog. This radiation fog usually forms during the overnight hours and early morning because that’s when conditions are right. passages.text: Fog is a cloud that forms at ground level when tiny water droplets, or sometimes ice crystals, become suspended in the air near Earth’s surface. It develops when air cools enough for water vapor to condense, or when moisture is added to the air until it becomes saturated. By scattering light, these tiny droplets reduce visibility and can make familiar landscapes, roads, and buildings difficult to see. Fog is a common weather phenomenon that can occur in nearly every part of the United States, from coastal regions and mountain valleys to agricultural plains and urban areas. Its formation depends on the interaction of temperature, humidity, wind, and the characteristics of the surrounding land or water. question: How are tunnels dug under rivers?
answer: Most underwater tunnels are either bored through soil or rock beneath the riverbed, or built from prefabricated sections floated into position and lowered into a prepared trench [1][2]. Many bored tunnels are excavated with a tunnel boring machine, which has a rotating cutterhead at the front [5]. passages.text: Underwater Tunnels Explained: How Engineers Build Tunnels Beneath Rivers and Seas Published on 25 November, 2026 | Updated on 25 November, 2026 Introduction Underwater tunnels are remarkable examples of modern civil engineering. They allow roads, railways, pedestrians and utility services to pass beneath rivers, lakes and seas without interrupting shipping or relying on bridges across the water. A common misconception is that underwater tunnels are built directly inside the water. In reality, most underwater crossings use one of two main construction methods. Some tunnels are excavated through soil or rock beneath the riverbed or seabed, while others are constructed from large prefabricated sections that are floated into position, lowered into a prepared trench and connected underwater. Both methods solve the same fundamental engineering challenge: creating a safe, stable and watertight passage while resisting groundwater pressure, soil loads and the surrounding geological conditions. The selection of a construction method depends on water depth, tunnel length, ground conditions, navigation requirements, environmental restrictions and project economics. For bored tunnels, the stability of the excavation face and control of groundwater inflow are major concerns. Unexpected fractures or weak geological zones can cause water ingress and ground loss. For immersed tube tunnels, trench preparation, element positioning, joint sealing and settlement control are particularly important. Marine construction also introduces challenges from currents, tides, waves, weather and underwater visibility. passages.text: Underwater tunnel An underwater tunnel is a tunnel which is partly or wholly constructed under the sea or a river. They are often used where building a bridge or operating a ferry link is unviable, or to provide competition or relief for existing bridges or ferry links.[1] While short tunnels are often road tunnels which may admit motorized traffic, unmotorized traffic or both, concerns with ventilation lead to the longest tunnels (such as the Channel Tunnel or the Seikan Tunnel) being electrified rail tunnels. Types of tunnel [edit] Various methods are used to construct underwater tunnels, including an immersed tube and a submerged floating tunnel. The immersed tube method involves steel tube segments that are positioned in a trench in the sea floor and joined together. The trench is then covered and the water pumped from the tunnel.[2] Submerged floating tunnels use the law of buoyancy to remain submerged, with the tunnel attached to the sea bed by columns or tethers, or hung from pontoons on the surface.[3] Advantages [edit] Compared with bridges [edit] One such advantage would be that a tunnel would still allow shipping to pass. passages.text: Prefer Tight, Low-Permeability Ground Permeability describes how easily water can pass through soil or rock. A highly permeable formation, such as coarse gravel, can allow groundwater to flow relatively freely. In contrast, dense clay or certain types of unfractured rock may have much lower permeability. For an underwater tunnel, low-permeability ground can reduce the amount of water entering the excavation. This makes it easier to maintain a controlled working environment and reduces the demands on pumping, groundwater control and waterproofing systems. The surrounding ground also contributes to tunnel stability by transferring loads around the excavated opening. However, its strength and behaviour must be evaluated carefully. A low-permeability layer is not automatically suitable for tunnelling. Engineers must also consider rock strength, deformation, faulting, swelling, squeezing behaviour and the possibility of water-bearing fractures. A strong but heavily fractured rock formation may still create serious groundwater problems. How a Tunnel Boring Machine Works Many modern underwater tunnels are excavated using a tunnel boring machine, commonly called a TBM. A TBM is a large mechanical system with a rotating cutterhead at the front. The cutterhead breaks or cuts the surrounding soil and rock as the machine advances. question: What physical problems make it harder to keep Moore's Law going as transistors shrink?
answer: As transistors approach atomic scales, quantum effects become a major restriction [3]. Electrons can leak past barriers through quantum tunneling, making transistor behavior inaccurate and unstable [3]. Heat dissipation is another issue, since packing transistors closer together raises temperatures inside the chip [3]. That heat can hurt dependability, reduce performance and increase energy consumption [3].

passages.title: What is Moore’s Law? - Our World in Data
passages.text: What is Moore’s Law? Exponential growth is at the heart of the rapid increase in computing capabilities. The observation that the number of transistors on computer chips doubles approximately every two years is known as Moore’s Law. Moore’s Law is not a law of nature, but an observation of a long-term trend in how technology is changing. The law was first described by Gordon E. Moore, the co-founder of Intel, in 1965.1 The chart shows Moore’s original graph that he drew in 1965 to describe this regularity. At the time, he had only a handful of data points. Note that he drew it on a logarithmic scale, and remember that a straight line on a log-axis means that the growth rate is constant, and it is therefore showing the exponential growth of the number of transistors. However, he hypothesized that this relationship would continue at a similar rate: “There is no reason to believe it will not remain constant for at least 10 years”.2 Moore’s Law has held true for more than half a century In 1965, Gordon Moore predicted that this growth would continue for another 10 years, at least.
